The Design Dash · Open-source design process

From a fuzzy problem to a plan people can use.

I designed The Design Dash to make a thorough product-design process more broadly available. It guides people through evidence, object modeling, and design decisions, then brings the work together in a plan with wireframes, technical requirements, and a way to validate what comes next.

Role
Process designer and author
Purpose
Make rigorous product planning easier to access
Foundation
OOUX, Object Guides, and a shared Object Library
Output
A connected plan for design, implementation, and validation

I — Inspiration

A finished screen can hide an unfinished idea

Generating an interface is fast. Establishing what it should do takes evidence, a clear product model, and considered decisions. When that reasoning stays in scattered notes and conversations, a polished screen can conceal unresolved assumptions.

I wanted The Design Dash to make that work approachable without reducing it to a prompt that produces screens. The intent is to help someone understand the problem, explore alternatives, and leave with a plan another person can inspect and use.

One simple example throughout

Imagine a neighborhood library that lends tools. Members need to find a tool, request to borrow it, and return it. This fictional Dash illustrates the method; its guides, wireframes, and rules are examples rather than findings from a real project.

D — Design Process

Start with the things people understand

Object-oriented UX (OOUX) provides the modeling foundation. Its ORCA process defines Objects, Relationships, Calls-to-action, and Attributes before turning them into navigation and screens. The tool-library example gives each object its own responsibility:

  • Tool records the item’s name and condition.
  • Member identifies the person borrowing it.
  • Loan connects the member and tool, records the due date, and moves from requested to checked out to returned.

Availability depends on the Loan, rather than being a label added independently to every screen.

Object Guides capture those definitions, including attributes, actions, relationships, lifecycle, business rules, and interface representations. They live in an Object Library, where future Dashes can reference them instead of rediscovering the same product concepts.

Reuse without silently changing the past

A Dash references a shared guide until it needs a different definition. It can then fork that guide locally and promote reviewed learning back into the library. This adds some record-keeping, but protects earlier work while allowing the library to grow.

E — Engagement

Guide the work without requiring one tool

A Dash begins with a problem, the people affected, the available evidence, and known constraints. Nine phases guide the work from opportunity and object modeling through flows, competing concepts, wireframes, and validation planning. Missing information stays visible as an assumption with a path to check it.

The same process can run in a general AI chat, a file-capable agent, or a facilitated workshop. The method defines the work and its review gates; adapters handle how each environment records it. A coded prototype is optional, so access to a development environment does not determine whether someone can create a useful plan.

Match the review to the consequences

Risk, reversibility, and reach determine the review tier. A small, reversible change needs less process than a consequential workflow. Every tier retains an ethics floor; higher-risk work keeps its required gates. AI critique can help uncover questions, but cannot replace accountable human review.

A — Action

Carry the same decision through every artifact

In the example Dash, one availability decision connects the plan:

  1. Requirement: show whether a tool can be borrowed.
  2. Object rule: allow one checked-out Loan per Tool.
  3. Wireframe: distinguish available and on-loan tools.
  4. Technical check: confirm availability again at checkout.
  5. Research: test whether members understand those states.

A complete plan, with room for unanswered questions

The Dash brings together:

  • Evidence, assumptions, opportunity framing, and success criteria.
  • Object Guides, relationships, scenario flows, and page architecture.
  • Concept comparisons, decision rationale, annotated wireframes, and edge states.
  • Functional and technical requirements, accessibility considerations, a research plan, and a stakeholder pitch.

One editable model; several useful views

I chose linked Markdown records as the Dash Model rather than making a rich document or database compulsory. The current Design Plan and release Story are generated views of those records. That keeps the work portable and reduces duplicate editing, with a tradeoff: links and required information need validation to prevent drift.

S — Status and next steps

Make the process useful beyond the person who ran it

The intended benefit is a shared reference: designers can follow a screen back to a decision, developers can find its behavior and constraints, and reviewers can see what is supported by evidence and what still needs testing. The Object Library preserves understanding for the next Dash.

I’m making The Design Dash open source so people can adapt the process to their own products and working environments. Its usefulness depends on the quality of the evidence and review people bring to it. A complete plan makes the next step clearer; it does not turn assumptions into validated results.

My design goal is to make the reasoning accessible along with the artifacts—so a team can decide what to build, why it matters, and how to learn whether it worked.
